title: Five counts and three proposals
note: Fictional unit. Figures are illustrative; PhilHealth rules and circulars in force, and your counsel and auditors, come first.
intro: You own a sixteen-station unit. At the monthly review, the manager shows the five counts for October: 540 sessions delivered, 531 fully documented, 516 claimed, 492 accepted, 478 paid. “We’re short 62 sessions of revenue,” she says. “I have some ideas.”

n1.prompt: What do you ask for first?

choices.text: The reasons at each drop, from the exceptions log: why 9 were not documented, 15 not claimed, 24 not accepted, and 14 accepted but not yet paid, and who owns each.
choices.feedback: Each count should equal the one before it; where it drops, there is a reason. The gap is leakage, and the fix is in the cause, not the number.

choices.text: Tell the team to push collections harder this month.
choices.feedback: Collections are the last step. Most of the gap starts earlier, in documentation and claiming, where pressure on collections does nothing.
choices.then: You ask for the reasons at each step instead.

choices.text: Look only at the 14 accepted but unpaid; that’s the money.
choices.feedback: That gap matters, but 48 sessions were lost before acceptance. Ask for all five steps.
choices.then: You ask for the reasons at every step.

n2.scene: The manager explains that nine sessions lack signed agreement forms. “We can have the patients sign now and date the forms to the session days.”

choices.text: No backdating. Check what the rules allow for late completion: if allowed, signatures dated today with an explanatory note, refiled within the period; if not, accept the loss. Then add a form check at the end of each session.
choices.feedback: A form signed today and dated to a past session is a false record, even if the session happened. A true claim filed late is a problem; a false claim filed on time is fraud.

choices.text: Approve it; the sessions really happened.
choices.feedback: That the session happened does not make a backdated signature true. It is a false record, and the owner who approves it carries the risk.
choices.then: Your counsel advises against it. You choose late completion dated today, where the rules allow.

choices.text: Write off all nine; it isn’t worth the effort.
choices.feedback: Some may be correctable within the rules. Check first, and fix the workflow either way.

n3.scene: “For the 24 not accepted,” the manager says, “a consultant says that if we change some diagnosis codes and session dates, more will pass.”

choices.text: Refuse. Have each non-accepted claim reviewed for its stated reason, corrected with true documentation and refiled where the rules allow, appealed with evidence, or written off with the cause fixed.
choices.feedback: Changing a date or diagnosis to fit a payment rule is falsification. Returned claims can usually be corrected and refiled; denied claims need a reason and a decision.

choices.text: Try it on a few claims and see what happens.
choices.feedback: A few false claims are still false claims, and they put the unit’s accreditation and the people who signed them at risk.
choices.then: You reject the idea and have each claim reviewed for its stated reason.

choices.text: Ask the consultant to put the advice in writing first.
choices.feedback: Written or not, the advice is to falsify claims. Decline it.

n4.scene: “Last idea: for denied sessions, we could charge the patients directly for what PhilHealth would have paid.”

choices.text: No: patients are not charged for what the package covers. The denials are the unit’s problem to fix.
choices.feedback: Charging a patient for what the benefit package covers crosses the integrity line. The patient was eligible and the session was delivered; the shortfall came from the unit’s process.

choices.text: Yes, but only for patients who can afford it.
choices.feedback: Selective charging is still charging for covered care, and it is unfair to the patients chosen.
choices.then: You reverse it before any patient is billed.

choices.text: Ask patients for a voluntary “donation” instead.
choices.feedback: A payment requested for covered care is a charge, whatever it is called.

n5.scene: The list shows 37 open claims; 11 are more than 90 days old. A typhoon last month led PhilHealth to issue a circular extending some filing periods.
n5.prompt: What do you put in place?

choices.text: Every open claim gets an age and an owner, reviewed monthly; one person is assigned to watch PhilHealth circulars and apply extensions; and the five counts with reasons come to every monthly review.
choices.feedback: A claim not followed up becomes a claim lost. Filing rules change, sometimes after disasters, so someone must watch them. Days to collect decides how much working capital the unit needs.

choices.text: Write off everything over 90 days and start fresh.
choices.feedback: Some old claims may still be within an extended period. Review them first.

choices.text: Ask the claims officer to work through the old ones when she has time.
choices.feedback: Without an owner per claim and a monthly review, “when she has time” becomes never.

end.title: Three months later
end.text: An end-of-session form check cut the documentation gap from 9 to 3. Intake now confirms PhilHealth Dialysis Database registration before a patient’s first session. No record was backdated, no code changed, and no patient was charged for covered care. The gap between delivered and paid fell from 62 to 29.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Five counts every month: delivered, documented, claimed, accepted, paid, with reasons at each drop.
  • Fix the cause, not the number.
  • The integrity line: never backdate, change a date or diagnosis, claim an undelivered session, or charge patients for covered care.
  • A true claim filed late is a problem; a false claim filed on time is fraud.
  • Every open claim has an age and an owner; someone watches the circulars.

See Session to cash, Fix the cause, Returned and denied claims and The integrity line.
